steps.scene: You're giving a friend's 11-year-old a lift. They're small for their age, well under 1.35 metres, and want the front seat.

options.text: A suitable child restraint
An adult seat belt — at 11 they're old enough
Nothing extra, as long as they sit in the back

question.explanation: Children need a child restraint until they're 12 or 1.35 metres tall, whichever comes first.

steps.title: Children are your job
steps.body: As the driver, you're legally responsible for making sure every passenger under 14 wears a seat belt or the right child restraint.

question.prompt: You're driving a neighbour's children, both under 14. Who must make sure they're belted in?

options.text: Their parents, even though they're not in the car
The children themselves
You, the driver

question.explanation: Passengers aged 14 and over are responsible for themselves. Under 14, it's on you.

steps.title: Baby seats and airbags
steps.body: Never fit a rear-facing baby seat in front of an active airbag. Deactivate the airbag first, or put the seat in the back.

question.prompt: The front passenger seat has an airbag. What must you do before fitting a rear-facing baby seat there?

options.text: Deactivate the airbag
Push the passenger seat as far back as it goes
Nothing — the airbag will protect the baby

question.explanation: An airbag inflates with enough force to cause serious injury to a baby in a rear-facing seat.

a.label: Heavy load on the roof
a.body: Raises the centre of gravity. The car is less stable, especially on bends and in wind.

b.label: Load secured
b.body: Strapped down with suitable restraints — ideally in a purpose-made roof box.

question.prompt: How will a heavy load on your roof rack affect the car?

options.text: It will make the car less stable
It will improve grip by pressing the tyres down
It makes no difference, if it's tied on

question.explanation: Weight high up makes the car lean and sway. Keep heavy items low, inside the car where you can.

steps.wrongBelief: If a vehicle is overloaded, it's the fault of whoever loaded it.

question.prompt: Who's responsible for making sure a vehicle isn't overloaded?

options.text: Whoever put the load on it
The driver
The hire company, if it's a hire van

question.explanation: An overloaded vehicle steers and brakes badly. The law holds the person driving it responsible.

steps.repairNote: The driver is responsible. Check the load and the vehicle's limits before you set off.

steps.scene: You're towing a caravan on a windy dual carriageway. A lorry overtakes and the caravan starts swinging from side to side.

options.text: Brake hard to stop it quickly
Accelerate to pull the caravan straight
Ease off the accelerator and let your speed fall

question.explanation: Snaking gets worse with speed. Easing off gently lets the caravan settle; harsh braking or steering can make it worse.

steps.title: Loading a trailer
steps.body: Spread the weight evenly, with the heaviest items over the trailer's axle. It cuts the risk of the trailer swerving or snaking.

question.prompt: How should you load a trailer?

options.text: With heavy items over the axles
With heavy items right at the back, away from the car
With the heaviest items on top, holding the rest down

question.explanation: Weight in the wrong place upsets the balance of the car and trailer together, and makes snaking far more likely.
